Hyper/Hypothermia
Mild to moderate nausea/vomiting
Administer ondansetron 4mg IV/IO/SL
May repeat ×1 after 10 minutes
Paramedic:
Severe nausea /vomiting that does not respond to Ondanestron:
Administer Droperidol 2.5mg IV/IO/IM
May repeat ×1
Basic Care:
Begin manual CPR
Apply AED and perform a rhythm analysis as soon as possible while limiting interruptions in CPR for analysis / shock period only
Insert blind supraglottic airway device (I-gel) and provide ventilations with continuous EtCO2 monitoring
Apply Lucas device after 2nd rhythm analysis/ shock period and set to deliver continuous compressions
Advanced Care:
Place patient on 3-lead ECG for continuous monitoring
Analyze patient at 2-minute intervals and follow AED prompts for defibrillation
Establish IV/IO access with isotonic crystalloid solution to keep vein open
Provide Epinephrine 1mg (1:10000) IV/ IO every 3-5 minutes for duration of arrest period
Initiate fluid bolus 500-1000 mL of isotonic crystalloid solution
Consider treatable causes such as overdose / poisoning
If suspected narcotic overdose
Provide 2 mg Naloxone IV/IO
If suspected hypoglycemia
Provide 25g Dextrose 50% IV/IO
For extended / unknown down-time
Provide Sodium Bicarbonate 1mEq/kg  IV/IO
Paramedic:
Perform rhythm analysis after every 2 minutes of continuous CPR
For ventricular fibrillation/ ventricular tachycardia
Defibrillate as soon as rhythm identified
Consider: Amiodarone for recurrent v-tach, Calcium for Hyperkalemia, Lidocaine if V-tach persists after Amiodarone, or Magnesium for Torsades.  See Pharmacopeia for more.
For Asystole or pulseless electrical activity
Continue CPR without defibrillation
Treat reversible causes
If ROSC achieved – follow ROSC protocol (See Page 38)
Perform endotracheal intubation and advanced airway management
After 20 minutes of care, determine whether transport is warranted ie there has been improvement, or a rhythm change from asystole or unwarranted follow Termination of Efforts protocol (See Page 10)
Indications:
Inadequate tissue perfusion manifesting as signs of hypoperfusion, including hypotension.
Basic Care:
Manage airway, breathing, and oxygenation as indicated.
For suspected trauma, fully expose patient and control external bleeding.
Place patient in supine position or recovery position as indicated and tolerated by patient.
Titrate oxygen to a SpO2 of >94%; for COPD patients, consider titrating to SpO2 of 88-92%.
Obtain complete set of vital signs; including SpO2 and blood glucose.  Consider additional testing (e.g., 12-lead ECG) and monitoring (e.g., capnography) as indicated.
Consider causes of shock that have specific treatment protocols, including:
Poisoning/Overdose
Anaphylaxis
Symptomatic bradycardia
Adrenal crisis (acute adrenal insufficiency)
Tension pneumothorax
Advanced Care:
- Initiate advanced airway management as indicated and be prepared for post-intubation hypotension.
- Fluid Resuscitation:
When indicated, administer 10-20 mL/kg of isotonic crystalloid solution IV/IO.  Repeat x1 as needed.  Contact medical control for additional fluid bolus orders.
Frequently reassess and titrate to resolved hypotension and improved perfusion (e.g., more alert, decreased capillary refill).
Discontinue fluids if patient develops sign/symptoms of volume overload (e.g., new/worsening tachypnea, SOA, decreasing SpO2, new/worsening rales/crackles).
Paramedic:
- Norepinephrine Infusion:
Consider norepinephrine infusion, when distributive shock (e.g., sepsis) is suspected, other causes with specific treatment protocols have been considered/utilized, if there’s no improvement of hypotension/hypoperfusion with fluid resuscitation or the patient continues to deteriorate.
Frequently reassess and titrate to resolved hypotension.
See infusion protocol (See Page 148)
-TXA:
If catastrophic hemorrhage of medical origin is present, such as active GI or vaginal bleeding
Administer TXA 2g IV/IO slow push
Special Considerations:
- Patients in 2nd/3rd trimester of pregnancy are at risk of developing supine hypotensive syndrome.  Consider placing in recovery position or manually displacing uterus to patient’s left.
- For shock resulting from trauma below the neck, especially penetrating trauma, consider titrating fluid resuscitation to the lower normal limit of the blood pressure range (e.g., 90 mmHg for 11-17 yo and adults).
- The elderly and patients taking cardiovascular medications (e.g., beta blockers, calcium channel blockers) have less compensatory tachycardia in response to shock and can deteriorate quickly.
- Adult patients with poorly controlled chronic HTN can have relative hypotension, which is a state of hypoperfusion at SBPs >90 mmHg.  Consider incrementally titrating to SBPs greater than 90 mmHg.
Basic Care:
Administer high-flow oxygen if tolerated.
Initiate EtCO2 monitoring via nasal cannula
Check for vaginal presentation
If normal delivery appears imminent, follow childbirth procedure (Page 102)
Look for signs/ symptoms of obstetrical complications and treat as indicated
Conditions that prompt immediate transport despite the threat of delivery include:
Prolonged membrane rupture (>24 hours)
Breech presentation
Cord presentation
Extremity (Limb) presentation
Evidence of meconium staining
Nuchal cord
Breech presentation
If the infant’s head does not deliver immediately, place a gloved hand in the vagina with the palm towards the infant’s face
With the index and middle fingers, form a “V” n either side of the infant’s nose
Prolapsed umbilical cord
Insert two fingers of a gloved hand to raise the presenting part of the fetus off of the cord
Positioning the mother in knee-chest position may relieve pressure on the cord
Instruct the mother to “pant” with each contraction to prevent her from bearing down
Nuchal cord
Examine the infant’s neck for the presence of a looped (nuchal) umbilical cord during delivery
If cord is looped around the neck, gently slip the cord over the infant’s head
If unable to do so, clamp and cut the cord
Provide repeated assessments to all patients
Advanced Care:
Establish IV/IO access with isotonic crystalloid solution to keep vein open
If newborn presents with signs/ symptoms of distress or hypoperfusion, follow the Newborn Resuscitation protocol (See Page 78)
Paramedic:
Eclamptic Seizures
Administer Magnesium Sulfate 4g IV/IO slow push over 3 minutes
Consider Midazolam 2mg IV/IO every 5 minutes until seizure activity stops OR 10mg IN
Catastrophic postpartum hemorrhage
Administer TXA 2g IV/IO slow push
Special Considerations:
Eclamptic seizures can occur up to 6 weeks postpartum but are most common 48 hours postpartum.
Most eclamptic seizures or signs of preeclampsia develop after 20 weeks gestation.
Signs of pre-eclampsia
Edema in the face, feet and/or hands.
Hypertension (systolic > 140 mmHg, diastolic >90 mmHg)
Headache
Blurred vision and or changes in vision
Eclampsia can occur without a previous diagnosis of pre-eclampsia.
Magnesium sulfate is the first line drug of choice when treating suspected eclamptic seizures
Pregnant patients or postpartum patients that are presenting with a blood pressure over 140 mmhg and/or diastolic over 90 mmhg or higher, coupled with other symptoms of preeclampsia should be treated with magnesium sulfate. These patients are at a high risk of progressing to eclampsia.
In the event of respiratory depression as a result of magnesium infusion the antidote is calcium chloride 1g IVP over 5 minutes.
Indications:
Recent cardiac arrest
Patient has palpable pulse
Patient’s mental status may range from awake/alert to unresponsive
Basic Care:
Continue to follow protocol covering presumptive cause of cardiac arrest
Maintain patent airway as needed and administer oxygen to correct potential hypoxia
Titrate to >92%
Initiate or maintain EtCO2 monitoring
Provide ventilatory support as needed (Avoid hyperventilation)
Keep defibrillator pads in place
Monitor vital signs frequently
Obtain 12-lead ECG and transmit to receiving facility if indicated
If hyperthermic, attempt passive cooling techniques
Advanced Care:
Establish IV/IO access if not already complete
Hypotension
Administer 250ml isotonic solution bolus
May repeat as necessary to maintain SBP >90mmHg
Obtain a blood glucose if not completed.  Treat hypoglycemia if indicated
Paramedic:
Maintain cardiac monitoring and treat dysrhythmias
Treat any reversible etiologies (H’s & T’s)
For continued hypoperfusion
Administer push dose epinephrine
20mcg every 3 minutes to total of 100mcg  OR
Administer Epinephrine infusion
See Page
Administer Norepinephrine infusion
See Page
Basic Care:
Titrate oxygen to a SpO2 of >94%; for COPD patients, consider titrating to SpO2 of 88-92%.
If signs of impending respiratory failure are present, initiate BVM assisted ventilation.
Optimize patient positioning (ear-to-sternal notch and if no spinal precautions needed consider raising head of bed to ~45 degrees).
Use two-person BVM ventilation whenever feasible.
Have oral suction available, preferably large bore catheter (e.g., DuCanto Catheter).
Utilize airway adjuncts, especially for patients with facial hair, obesity, no teeth or protruding teeth.
Initiate EtCO2 monitoring and use to optimize BVM ventilation rate
Follow other protocols as appropriate, including:
Asthma/ COPD CHF/ Pulmonary Edema Shock/ Hypoperfusion
Allergic Reaction Poisoning/Overdose Hypoglycemia
Advanced Care:
Initiate cardiac monitoring
Establish IV access
Paramedic:
Consider reversible cause of patient presentation, including tension pneumothorax (see thoracostomy procedure page 109), opioid overdose, hypoglycemia.
For impending respiratory failure or anticipated loss of airway control (patient’s ability to protect airway), consider advanced airway management:
Nasotracheal intubation indications include:
Spontaneously breathing, unable to achieve sufficient facial / airway muscle relaxation, no sign traumatic facial instability.
Orotracheal intubation indications include:
Unconscious, no gag reflex, high risk for aspiration.
Time permitting, consider correcting hypotension (e.g., fluid bolus under pressure) prior to intubation.
Utilize airway management techniques (see Basic Treatment section) and consider oxygenating with two high flow sources (e.g., BVM and NC) to optimize SpO2 prior to and between intubation attempts.
Video laryngoscopy (VL) is to be used, unless equipment is damaged, not functioning correctly, or an appropriate size VL blade is not available.
The gum elastic bougie markedly improves oral intubation success rates and it’s routine use is strongly encouraged.
For placement of an endotracheal tube, an intubation attempt is defined as insertion of the laryngoscope blade into the mouth or endotracheal tube into the naris (opening of nose).
Intubation attempt durations should be no greater than 30 seconds and should be stopped sooner if marked SpO2 drop occurs during the intubation attempt.
Prior to further attempts, consider causes of failed attempt including:
Poor patient positioning
Need for different style of laryngoscope blade
Need for bougie
Facial / airway muscle tone too pronounced for oral intubation attempt in adult (need sedation)
If intubation unsuccessful after 3 attempts consider placing blind airway insertion device (BIAD), like the iGel.
Drug Assisted Intubation
RESTRICTED – GRADE 2 PARAMEDIC OR ABOVE ONLY
If unable to orally intubate adult patient due to facial/airway muscle tone and patient is at risk of aspiration or airway cannot be managed another way aside from intubation:
Consider drug assisted intubation (DAI) with Etomidate dose 0.3 mg/kg IV/IO (Max dose 20 mg) OR Ketamine 1.5mg/kg IV/IO
If insufficient relaxation, may repeat Etomidate at 0.1 mg/kg IV/IO. OR Ketamine at 1.5mg/kg IV/IO
If unable to intubate and unable to oxygenate / ventilate with BVM or BIAD, consider percutaneous cricothyrotomy
If sedation is required after successful intubation procedure and patient is     not hypotensive:
Consider Midazolam:
IV/IO:
Adult: 2-4 mg (Repeat in 10 minute intervals as needed)
Pediatric: 0.15 mg/kg (max single dose 4 mg)
IM/IN:
Adult: 10 mg
Pediatric: 0.15 mg/kg (max single dose 4 mg)
Repat IV/IO or IM/IN dose x1 in 5 minutes, as needed.
If Midazolam is not available, consider Lorazepam:
IV/IO:
Adult: 2 mg
Pediatric: 0.15 mg/kg (max single dose 2 mg)
After securing the advanced airway and verifying placement, attach device to ventilator utilizing Ventilator Protocol settings (Reference Page 102)
Rapid Sequence Intubation:
RESTRICTED – GRADE 3 PARAMEDIC ONLY
If all of the above procedures have failed to adequately manage and maintain the airway and it cannot be managed by other means, consider Rapid Sequence Intubation (RSI).
Cardiac monitoring, pulse oximetry, blood pressure, and continuous EtCO2 are required and must be documented.
All monitoring equipment should be placed prior to, during, and after any airway procedure
Pre-oxygenation
Position the patient supine in the sniffing position
Elevate the occiput so that the ears and sternal notch are parallel to the floor
Regardless of SpO2, place spontaneously breathing patients on a Non-Rebreather @ 15LPM
EtCO2 should be attached to the BVM circuit when in use
Preparation
Assemble all equipment (e.g. suction, BVM, CMAC, ET tube, bougie, stylet, SGA)
Establish and ensure patent IV/IO
Prepare Etomidate 0.3mg/kg
Prepare Midazolam 2mg
Prepare Succinylcholine 1.5 mg/kg
Assign team roles and perform verbal walkthrough of treatment plan
Apply nasal cannula 15lpm
Do not use a side-stream EtCO2 device
Induction
Administer Etomidate 0.3 mg/kg IV/IO AND Midazolam 2 mg IV/IO and flush with normal saline
Immediately administer Succinylcholine 1.5 mg/kg IV/IO and flush with normal saline
Continue to deliver pre-oxygenation during medication onset (45-90) seconds
Once the jaw is flaccid, perform laryngoscopy
If SpO2 drops below 93%, ventilate and oxygenate with SGA
Second attempt may be made once SpO2 is above 93%
If SGA unsuccessful, ventilate with two-handed BVM
If unable to oxygenate with the BVM, perform cricothyrotomy per protocol
Post-procedure
Confirm tube placement with EtCO2
If there is no waveform, the intubation is unsuccessful
Remove the tube and ventilate with SGA/ BVM
Assess for bilateral breath sounds
Secure tube with commercial device or twill tie
Document the depth of the tube at the teeth
If all other measures have failed to secure the airway and it cannot be maintained via other means for reasons such as:
Complete airway obstruction above the level of the cricothyroid membrane
Consider needle cricothyroidotomy (See page 104)
Basic Care:
Administer oxygen
Titrate to >92% and improved work of breathing
Initiate continuous EtCO2 monitoring
Position patient to avoid injury and / or aspiration
Consider placing patient in lateral recumbent position
Determine blood glucose concentration
Follow diabetic emergency protocol if indicated
Follow other protocols as appropriated for:

Once the body is fully delivered, dry the infant and wrap in a thermal blanket or dry towel. Cover the infant’s scalp.
Assess breathing
If breathing is inadequate, stimulate the infant by gently rubbing the back and flicking the soles of the feet
If breathing is still inadequate after stimulation, begin assisted ventilation via BVM at a rate of 40-60 breaths per minute
If breathing is adequate, but the infant displays central cyanosis, administer high-flow oxygen via blow-by
Assess heart rate by auscultation or by palpation of the umbilical cord stump.  If less than 60 beats per minute:
Assist ventilations
Begin chest compressions at a rate of 120 per minute (3 compressions to each ventilation)
If the heart rate is still less than 60 bpm after 30 seconds of chest compressions:
Consider insertion of supraglottic rescue airway device
Advanced Care:
If the heart rate is still less than 60 bpm after 30 seconds of chest compressions:
Establish IV/IO access with isotonic crystalloid to keep vein open
Administer epinephrine (1:10000) 0.01mg/kg  IV/IO
May repeat every 5 minutes to max total of 4 doses
Paramedic:
If meconium is present, initiate endotracheal intubation before the infant takes its first breath
Suction the airway using a meconium aspirator while withdrawing the tube
Repeat the procedure until the tube is clear of meconium
If the infant’s heart rate slows, immediately discontinue suctioning and ventilate the infant
If the infant is already breathing, intubation and suctioning may be omitted
Consider endotracheal intubation if heart rate remains below 60bpm

Febrile seizure suspected:
Obtain temperature, if possible, and remove excess clothing/ blankets
Advanced Care:
Establish IV/IO access with isotonic crystalloid solution to keep vein open
Paramedic:
Monitor carefully for respiratory depression and need for assisted ventilation as appropriate
Consider airway adjuncts
Actively seizing:
Administer Midazolam 0.15 mg/kg (max 2mg) IV/IO/IM/IN

protocols.title: Pediatric Trauma
protocols.content:
Guidelines
Basic Care:
Consult age-based guide such as Handtevy app for appropriate medication doses/interventions/equipment sizes and references to normal vital sign ranges for pediatric patients
Administer oxygen
Titrate to >95% and improved work of breathing
Initiate continuous EtCO2 monitoring
Control bleeding with direct pressure and elevation if possible
Cover the stump with moist, sterile gauze then wrap with dry dressing
Wrap the severed part in a saline moistened sterile dressing
Place in a watertight plastic bag
Place the bag in a cooler with ice if possible
Do not place directly in ice or submerge/ soak in water
Do not freeze
Advanced Care:
Assess for hemodynamic instability
Establish IV/IO access with isotonic crystalloid solution to keep vein open
Paramedic:
Consider pain management protocol in isolated injury
Administer Fentanyl 1mcg/kg IV/IO  OR  1.5mcg/kg IN
Max single dose 50mcg
May repeat x
OR
Administer Ketamine 0.3 mg/kg IV/IO
May repeat x
Basic Care:
Consult age-based guide such as Handtevy app for appropriate medication doses/interventions/equipment sizes and references to normal vital sign ranges for pediatric patients
Administer oxygen
Titrate to >95% and improved work of breathing
Initiate continuous EtCO2 and cardiac monitoring
Begin airway management as appropriate
Obtain 12-lead ECG, especially when injury involves electrical burns
Monitor CO level if possible
Stop the burning process
Remove dry chemicals and flush affected area with copious amounts of water
Remove contaminated clothing
Remove clothing and jewelry in the area of the burn and distal to the injured area
For chemical burns of the eye, flush the eyes with copious amounts of water or saline
Attempt to cool the affected area
Prevent heat loss below normal body temperature and monitor for hypothermia
Determine blood glucose concentration
Estimate total body surface area (TBSA) affected and depth of the burns
1st degree burns are not included in TBSA
Apply dry dressing to burns as tolerated
Advanced Care:
Establish IV/IO access with isotonic crystalloid solution to keep vein open
Lactated ringers to be administered
5 years and younger: 125 mL per hour initial fluid resuscitation
6-13 years: 250 mL per hour initial fluid resuscitation
IVs may be inserted through the burn tissue if necessary
Paramedic:
Consider Pediatric Pain Management protocol
Administer Fentanyl 1mcg/kg IV/IO  OR  1.5 mcg/kg IN
Max single dose 50 mcg
May repeat x
OR
Administer Ketamine 0.3 mg/kg IV/IO
May repeat x
Begin advanced airway management as appropriate
Observe for signs of inhalation injury (stridor, muffled voice, carbonaceous sputum)
If signs of inhalation injury are present, prepare to secure the airway
Basic Care:
Consult age-based guide such as Handtevy app for appropriate medication doses/interventions/equipment sizes and references to normal vital sign ranges for pediatric patients
Transport/ assess patient in upright sitting position
Reassess frequently for airway patency
Visually inspect teeth, tongue, and oral mucosa for deformity, bleeding, laceration, fracture etc.
Use great caution if you choose to place fingers in the patient’s mouth during examination
Control minor bleeding with a small piece of gauze held by the patient
Suction as needed to clear airway
Bleeding post-tonsillectomy (5-7 days after surgery):
Bleeding may be severe and is a surgical emergency
Consider direct pressure with gauze if possible
May use gauze wrapped around Magill forceps

protocols.title: Epinephrine
protocols.content:
Indicated for anaphylaxis with airway/respiratory involvement or hypotension with exposure to known allergen.
<30 kg: 0.15 mg of 1:1,000 concentration IM.  Repeat up to 2 times every 5-10 minutes, as needed.
≥30 kg: 0.30 mg of 1:1,000 concentration IM.  Repeat up to 2 times every 5-10 minutes, as needed.
Contact medical control for additional doses.
- Nebulized Albuterol:
Indicated for wheezing/bronchospasm.
2.5 mg Albuterol (0.5% concentration) nebulized.  Repeat up to 3 times every 5-10 minutes, as needed.
Advanced Care:
Establish IV/IO access with isotonic crystalloid solution to keep vein open
Paramedic:
Initiate advanced airway management as indicated and anticipate airway will be difficult to manage.

protocols.title: Epinephrine
protocols.content:
Indicated for anaphylaxis with airway/respiratory involvement or hypotension with exposure to known allergen or recent (minutes) exposure to know allergen with high-risk features (e.g., history of near fatal or biphasic anaphylaxis, asthma/COPD, cardiovascular disease).
Patient weight <30 kg: 0.15 mg of 1:1,000 concentration IM.  Repeat up to 2 times every 5-10 minutes, as needed.
Patient weight ≥30 kg: 0.30 mg of 1:1,000 concentration IM.  Repeat up to 2 times every 5-10 minutes, as needed.
Contact medical control for additional doses.
- Epinephrine Infusion:
Anaphylaxis with impending airway/respiratory compromise or cardiovascular collapse or profound shock/hypotension that’s refractory to ≥2 IM epinephrine doses and fluid bolus.
Patient weight <30 kg: infuse at 0.1-1.0 mcg/min. (see Epinephrine Infusion protocol P. 133)
Patient weight ≥30 kg: infuse at 1.0-10.0 mcg/min (see Epinephrine Infusion protocol P. 133).
- Nebulized Albuterol / Ipratropium:
Indicated for wheezing /bronchospasm.
2.5 mg albuterol (0.5% concentration) and 0.5 mg ipratropium (0.02% concentration) nebulized.
Repeat albuterol treatments up to 3 times every 5-10 minutes, as needed.
- Fluid Resuscitation:
When indicated, administer 10-20 mL/kg isotonic crystalloid fluid bolus IV/IO (repeat x1 as needed).
Contact medical control for additional fluid bolus orders.
Frequently reassess and titrate to resolved hypotension and improved perfusion (e.g., more alert, decreased capillary refill).
Discontinue fluids if patient develops sign/symptoms of volume overload (e.g., new/worsening tachypnea, SOA, decreasing SpO2, new/worsening rales/crackles).

protocols.title: Diphenhydramine
protocols.content:
Indicated for skin signs/symptoms.  Should never delay administration of epinephrine.
1 mg/kg IV/IO/IM.  Max dose 50 mg.
- Methylprednisolone:
Relatively slow-acting medication that can be considered for in addition to other therapies.  Should never delay administration of Epinephrine.
2 mg/kg IV/IO.
Patient weight <30 kg: max dose 60 mg.
Patient weight ≥30 kg: max dose 125 mg
-Note: Beta blockers and ace inhibitors may exacerbate anaphylaxis symptoms
Indications:
Exposure to toxic substances from:
○ Ingestion
○ Inhalation
○ Injection
○ Skin absorption
○ Intentional/accidental exposure to pharmacological substances
Other medical conditions (see below) causing altered mental status
Basic Care:
Remove patient from toxic environment as quickly as possible, remove clothing, and decontaminate if applicable
○ This should be performed by trained personnel with appropriate PPE
Administer oxygen
○ Titrate to ≥92% and work of breathing
○ Assist ventilations as appropriate
Initiate continuous EtCO2 monitoring
Follow other protocols as appropriate
○ Diabetic Emergencies
○ Hypothermia/Hyperthermia
○ Seizures/Status Epilepticus
○ Stroke/CVA/TIA
○ Trauma
○ Agitated/Aggressive Patient
Use patient and/or bystander statements and answers to determine if/what substances are involved
Determine blood glucose concentration and if <60mg/dL
○ Administer oral glucose 15g buccal, if conscious and able to tolerate
▪ If unable to tolerate oral glucose AND PATIENT HAS A PRESCRIPTION
▪ Administer Glucagon 1mg IM
Suspected opiate/opioid overdose
○ Administer Naloxone 2-4mg IN
May administer additional 2-4mg IN every 5 minutes to restore respiratory drive to max total 8mg
Suspected carbon monoxide exposure
○ Monitor CO level if possible
○ Administer high-flow oxygen at 15LPM
Advanced Care:
Establish IV/IO access with isotonic crystalloid solution to keep vein open
Blood glucose concentration is <60mg/dL
○ Administer Dextrose 50% or D-10, 25g IV/IO
May repeat x1 if no response
IV access cannot be obtained
○ Administer Glucagon 1mg IM
Suspected opiate/opioid overdose
○ Administer Naloxone 2mg IV every 5 minutes to restore respiratory drive to max total 8mg
Paramedic Care:
Begin advanced airway management as appropriate
Initiate cardiac monitoring
If signs of shock refer to shock protocols
Patient exhibits signs of organophosphate poisoning
○ Administer Atropine 2mg IV/IO
Repeat at 4mg every 3 minutes fully atropinized (secretions dried)
Suspected TCA overdose
○ Administer Sodium Bicarbonate 100mEq IV/IO
Suspected beta-blocker overdose
○ Administer Glucagon 3mg IV/IO
May repeat x1 at 2mg
Suspected calcium channel-blocker overdose
○ Administer Calcium Chloride 1g IV/IO every 5 minutes to max total 3g
Suspected dystonic reaction
○ Administer Diphenhydramine 50mg IV/IO/IM
Suspected adrenal crisis
AMS, hypoglycemia, hypotension, seizures, arrhythmias
Administer Solu-Medrol 125mg IV/IO/IM
Indications:
Exacerbation of previously diagnosed asthma or COPD
Characterized by some combination of:
▪ Wheezing
▪ Tachypnea
▪ Accessory muscle use/retraction
▪ Inability to speak in full sentences
Wheezing due to suspected asthma or suspected COPD
Basic Care:
Administer oxygen
○ Titrate to ≥ 92% and work of breathing unless COPD history
Oxygen administration in COPD patients:
○ Patient with history of COPD may have normal lower baseline oxygen saturation; do not automatically place on high-flow oxygen
○ Start 2-3LPM oxygen via nasal cannula
○ Titrate to patient’s baseline oxygen saturation or 88-92% and work of breathing
Initiate continuous EtCO2 monitoring
Acquire and transmit 12-lead EKG per 12-lead EKG procedure
Wheezing /bronchospasm
○ Administer 0.5% Albuterol 2.5mg with 0.02% Ipratropium Bromide 0.5mg nebulized
▪ May repeat x1
Advanced Care:
Establish IV/IO access with isotonic crystalloid solution to keep vein open
In addition to EMT DuoNeb, the AEMT may administer:
○ Additional DuoNeb treatments every 5 minutes as long as wheezing is present
Initiate cardiac monitoring
For moderate to severe respiratory distress
○ Initiate CPAP, per CPAP procedure
Discontinue CPAP if patient becomes hypotensive (SBP <100mmHg) Clinical picture worsens or initial presentation of impending respiratory failure
Paramedic Care:
For severe respiratory distress that does not respond to previously indicated treatments.
Follow protocol for Respiratory Distress or Failure/Drug Assisted Intubation (See Page 39)
○ Initiate ventilations via BVM
For Subacute presentation
○ Administer Methylprednisolone 125mg IV/IO
○ Administer Magnesium Sulfate 2g IV slow push or for infusion (See Page 140)
Unable to cooperate or otherwise tolerate nebulizer therapy or impending respiratory failure
○ Administer Epinephrine (1:1,000) 0.3mg IM
May repeat after 5 minutes
Impending respiratory failure
Initiate advanced airway management per Respiratory Distress or Failure/Drug Assisted Intubation protocol (See Page 39)
Indications:
Heart rate less than 60 beats per minute with signs of hypoperfusion, including hypotension. Rates less than 50 beats per minute are more likely to be associated with hypoperfusion.
Basic Care:
Place patient in supine or recovery position as indicated and tolerated by patient.
Obtain complete set of vital signs; including SpO2, blood glucose, and 12-lead ECG.
Titrate oxygen to a SpO2 of >94%; for COPD patients, consider titrating to SpO2 of 88-92%.
If signs of impending respiratory failure are present, initiate BVM assisted ventilation.
Advanced Care:
Initiate 3-lead ECG monitoring and consider early application of defibrillator/pacing pads.
Establish IV/IO with isotonic crystalloid to keep vein open
Paramedic:
Initiate advanced airway management as indicated and be prepared for post-intubation hypotension and/or worsening bradycardia.
Transcutaneous pacing:
Indicated for severe hypoperfusion +/- 2nd degree Mobitz II or 3rd degree heart block.  If present, don’t delay transcutaneous pacing (TCP) for IV placement or medication administration.
Consider sedation prior to TCP, if the patient isn’t at risk of impending cardiovascular collapse, or if purposeful movement affects ability to pace
Midazolam 2mg IV or 10mg IN  - May repeat x 1 in 10 minutes to maintain sedation
Initial settings:
Mode: sync/demand
Rate: 80 bpm
Current: start low and increase by 5-10 mA until mechanical capture is achieved (usually 40-80 mA).
Additional considerations:
Generally, the heart rate setting of 80 bpm is enough to produce adequate perfusion.
If capture is not achieved at current of 110 mA, consider repositioning pads and additional/alternative treatments.

protocols.title: Atropine
protocols.content:
1 mg IV/IO.  Repeat x2 every 3-5 minutes, as needed.
Atropine is indicated for symptomatic bradycardia due to increased vagal tone +/- 1st degree heart block.
Ineffective for heart transplant patients, bradycardia due to hypoxia, 3rd degree heart block, and usually 2nd degree heart block.
- Fluid Resuscitation:
IV fluids can be used to treat hypotension (see Hypoperfusion Protocol Page 35), but should not delay or replace treatments that directly target suspected causes of bradycardia (e.g., atropine for increased vagal tone).
When indicated, administer 10-20 mL/kg isotonic crystalloid fluid bolus IV/IO (repeat x1 as needed).  Contact medical control for additional fluid bolus orders.
Consider Norepinephrine for persistent hypotension in the unstable patient (Reference protocol Page 148)
- Situations where additional/alternative treatments are often needed, include:
Beta blocker overdose:
Glucagon 2 mg IV/IO given over 1 minute.  Repeat dose x2 every 3-5 minutes, as needed.  Contact medical control for additional doses.
Calcium channel blocker overdose:
Calcium chloride 1 gm IV/IO slow IVP.
Hyperkalemia:
Calcium chloride 1 gm IV/IO slow IVP.
Sodium bicarbonate (8.4% solution) 1 mEq/kg IV/IO.  Repeat x1 in 5-10 minutes, as needed.
Severe / prolonged acidosis or sodium channel blocker overdose:
Sodium bicarbonate (8.4% solution) 1 mEq/kg IV/IO.  Repeat x1 in 5-10 minutes, as needed.
Symptomatic bradycardia refractory to TCP and/or other treatments:
Consider epinephrine infusion 2-10 mcg/min (see Epinephrine Infusion protocol page 133)
or
Consider push-dose Epinephrine 20 mcg slow IVP over 2 minutes.  Repeat every 3-5 minutes, as needed
Indications:
- Respiratory distress in a patient with ≥1 of the following:
Clinical appearance of volume overload.
Suspected flash pulmonary edema / diffuse rales on exam.
History of congestive heart failure (CHF) with symptoms that feel similar.
History suggestive of volume overload (e.g., CHF patient that missed dialysis).
- The absence of peripheral edema does not rule out acute CHF exacerbation.
Contraindications:
Systolic blood pressure (SBP) <100 mmHg (consider cardiogenic shock).
Clinical appearance suggesting asthma / COPD exacerbation.
Serious infection / sepsis
Basic Care:
Titrate oxygen to a SpO2 of >94%; for COPD patients, consider titrating to SpO2 of 88-92%.
If signs of impending respiratory failure are present, initiate BVM assisted ventilation.
Obtain 12-lead ECG.
If chest pain or anginal-equivalent are present, follow Acute Coronary Syndrome protocol (See Page 29)
If appropriate, call for advanced life support, but do not delay transport.
If severe wheezing is present, consider nebulized albuterol 2.5 mg.
May repeat in 5-15 minutes as needed.
Advanced Care:
Initiate EtCO2 monitoring.
Initiate cardiac monitoring.
If severe wheezing is present, consider nebulized albuterol 2.5 mg with ipratropium 0.5 mg.
May repeat albuterol every 5-15 minutes as needed, for a total of up to 3 additional doses.
If moderate to severe respiratory distress is present:
Initiate CPAP, as per CPAP procedure:
If signs of impending respiratory failure develop prior to or following initiation of CPAP, proceed to assist ventilations with BVM.
Discontinue CPAP if patient develops hypotension.
Establish IV access.
Paramedic:
Treat dysrhythmia as appropriate.
Administer nitroglycerin (NTG) and titrate to SBP:
SBP >160 mmHg: 0.8 mg SL NTG every 5 minutes up to 3 total doses.
SBP 100-160 mmHg: 0.4 mg SL NTG every 5 minutes.
Assess blood pressure prior to repeat doses.
Do not administer NTG if patient has taken an erectile dysfunction medication (e.g., Sildenafil) within the last 48 hours.
Do not administer NTG if the patient is currently on an IV infusion for pulmonary hypertension.
If signs of impending respiratory failure are present, initiate BVM assisted ventilation and advanced airway management per Respiratory arrest/ failure/ DAI protocol. (Page 39)
*** Special Considerations ***
Assisting ventilations with BVM is indicated for patients with severe respiratory distress / severe hypoxia and not tolerating CPAP, peri-arrest state, or inadequate respiratory rate or tidal volume.
Multiple oxygen sources can be used to achieve desired SpO2 readings (CPAP + inline nebulizer or Non Rebreather Mask + NC).
Non-cardiogenic pulmonary edema (e.g., irritant exposure, post-opioid overdose) are not likely to benefit from nitroglycerin unless markedly hypertensive.
Indications:
Patient has a clinically significant glucose reading with an acute altered mental status.
Basic Care:
Administer oxygen
Titrate to >92% and improved work of breathing
Initiate continuous ETCO2 monitoring
Determine blood glucose concentration
Relatively or clinically hypoglycemic, without concern of aspiration
Administer oral glucose 15g buccal until mental status improves
May repeat every 5 minutes as needed
Advanced Care / Paramedic:
Patient is unable to tolerate oral glucose administration
Establish IV/ IO access with isotonic crystalloid solution to keep vein open
Initiate cardiac monitoring
For hypoglycemia
Administer Dextrose 50% (or Dextrose 10%) 25g IV/IO
If IV/IO access cannot be obtained
Administer Glucagon 1mg IM
For hyperglycemia
Consider 250-500 ML bolus of isotonic crystalloid for patient with severe hyperglycemia as appropriate to respiratory status (if no signs/ symptoms of pulmonary edema)
Indications:
-Elevated body temperature related to heat exposure
-Altered mental status related to heat exposure
Mild Symptoms
Heat cramps, Heat exhaustion
No signs of altered mental status
Body temperature <104⁰F
Diaphoresis
Severe Symptoms
Altered mental status
Body temperature >104⁰F
Sweating may have stopped
Basic Care:
Administer oxygen
Titrate to >92% and improved work of breathing
Initiate ETCO2 monitoring
Determine blood glucose concentration
Move patient to a cool place away from any external heat source if possible
Obtain patient temperature (Core temperature is preferred if obtainable)
Mild Symptoms:
Help facilitate passive cooling
Loosen clothing and remove excessive clothing
Administer PO fluids if available
Use caution if patient presents with nausea/ vomiting
Severe Symptoms:
Begin active cooling
On scene cold water immersion if possible
In transport continue cooling with directed air conditioning and cooled towels
Create mobile ice bath if possible (body bag filled with ice)
Place ice packs behind the neck, in arm-pits, and groin
If shivering starts, temperature drops below 102⁰ F, or AMS improves, stop active cooling
Advanced Care/ Paramedic:
Establish IV/ IO access with isotonic crystalloid solution to keep vein open
Initiate IV/IO bolus of 500 ml for hypotension
May repeat up to max of 2L
Indications:
Decreased body temperature related to cold exposure
Altered mental status related to cold exposure
Repeated ACLS medications and repeated defibrillations are ineffective below 86º F (core temperature)
Basic Care:
Administer oxygen
Titrate to ≥92% and improved work of breathing
Initiate continuous EtCO2 monitoring
Acquire 12-lead EKG if indicated
Decrease ongoing heat loss as soon as possible
Move the patient to a warm area
Dry and insulate the patient
Handle the patient gently allowing the patient no exertion
Rough handling of a severely hypothermic patient may cause ventricular fibrillation
Remove all wet clothing (cut off to decrease patient movement)
Initiate passive external rewarming with blankets in a warm ambulance
Conscious patients should avoid heated oral fluids
Suspected severe hypothermia
Assess respirations and pulse carefully as both may be very slow but still adequate for the patient’s slow metabolism
Provide expeditious, non-emergency transport
Advanced Care / Paramedic:
Severe hypothermia
Begin airway management as appropriate
Establish IV/IO access with isotonic crystalloid solution to keep vein open
Cardiac arrest
If a shockable rhythm is present, administer only one defibrillatory shock
Administer epinephrine (1:10,000) 1mg x1
Continue BLS CPR
If restored to a perfusing rhythm, follow the appropriate protocol
Indications:
Non-traumatic chest pain suspicious for Acute Coronary Syndrome
Angina/myocardial infarction
Anginal equivalent symptoms (typically in the presence of risk factors for, or prior history of, Coronary Artery Disease)
Dyspnea (with or without exertion)
Light-headedness
Generalized weakness
Syncope or near syncope
Diaphoresis
Nausea and/or vomiting
Maintain a high index of suspicion for atypical presentations, e.g., diabetic patients or females
For any patient under 18 years of age, or for any patient being transported to a primary pediatric facility, MEDICAL CONTROL MUST BE CONTACTED PRIOR TO THE ADMINISTRATION OF ASPIRIN OR NITROGLYCERIN
Basic Care:
Administer oxygen
Titrate to ≥92% and improved work of breathing
Initiate continuous EtCO2 monitoring
Acquire and transmit 12-lead EKG, per 12-lead EKG procedure
Administer aspirin 324mg PO (to be chewed)
Do not withhold unless known allergy or history of anaphylaxis
Administer nitroglycerin
If the patient has previously been prescribed, assist with administration 0.4mg SL every 5 minutes (Max 3 doses for BLS)
Titrate to SBP>100 and signs/symptoms (recheck BP before each dose)
DO NOT ADMINISTER if erectile dysfunction medications have recently been used
Advanced Care:
Establish IV/IO access with isotonic crystalloid solution to keep vein open
Consider 250-500mL fluid bolus for borderline or relative hypotension
Administer nitroglycerin 0.4mg SL every 5 minutes
Titrate to SBP>90 and signs/symptoms
DO NOT ADMINISTER if erectile dysfunction medications have recently been used
Severe nausea/vomiting
Administer ondansetron 4mg IV/IO/SL
May repeat ×1 after 10 minutes
Paramedic:
Initiate continuous cardiac monitoring
Consider right-sided, 15-lead ECG, and/or posterior ECG if necessary
Severe nausea/vomiting
Administer ondansetron 4mg IV/IO/SL
May repeat ×1 after 10 minutes
Consider Droperidol 2.5mg IV/IO/IM if ondansetron is ineffective at relieving nausea/vomiting
Pre-activation of the cath-lab if appropriate
Transport to PCI capable facility for presenting STEMI or suspected Non-STEMI
Basic Care:
Gently position the patient to facilitate airway
Suction as necessary
Advanced Care:
Establish IV/IO access with isotonic crystalloid solution to keep vein open
Signs/symptoms of volume depletion
Consider administration of 250-500mL bolus of isotonic crystalloid solution IV/IO
May repeat ×1
Consider possible causes and follow other protocols as appropriate:
Ischemic Chest Pain/ACS/STEMI
Head Trauma

protocols.title: Ibuprofen
protocols.content: Single dose of 400-800mg taken PO    OR

protocols.title: Acetaminophen
protocols.content:
Single dose of 500-1000 mg taken PO
Advanced Care:
Establish IV/IO access with isotonic crystalloid solution to keep vein open
Paramedic:
Patients receiving the medications listed below should be closely observed with monitoring of BP, Heart rate, EtCO2, airway patency, breathing status, and circulation.
Severe pain:

protocols.title: Fentanyl
protocols.content:
IV/IO: 1 mcg/kg slow push
Adult max single dose 100 mcg.
Pediatric max single dose 50 mcg
IM/IN: 1.5 mcg/kg
Repeat IV or IM/IN doses every 3-5 minutes, as needed.
Adult max total 150 mcg.
Pediatric max total 100 mcg.
Contact medical control for additional doses.

protocols.title: Ketamine
protocols.content:
IV/IO: 0.25 mg/kg, (dilute dose in 10 mL saline and administer IVP over 3-5 minutes)
Adult/Pediatric max single dose 25 mg.
IM/IN: 1 mg/kg.
Adult/Pediatric max single dose 100 mg.
Repeat IV or IM/IN dose x1 in 10 minutes, as needed.
Contact medical control for additional doses.
Special Considerations:
Coadministration (never in same syringe) of Ketamine and Fentanyl may enhance the beneficial effects of these medications but may also enhance adverse effects like respiratory depression.
For narcotic associated nausea and vomiting, administer ondansetron 0.1 mg / kg IV/IO (max dose 4 mg)
For respiratory depression associated with fentanyl treatment, manage the airway / breathing and administer naloxone 0.4-2 mg IV/IO/IM/IN titrated to respiratory status.
Basic Care:
Ensure the airway is patent while protecting the cervical spine
Evaluate for and treat exsanguinating hemorrhage
Initiate oxygen therapy with continuous EtCO2 monitoring
Begin airway management as appropriate
Treat injuries and control bleeding as needed including wound packing, and / or tourniquet application
Determine the need for C-Spine immobilization per selective spinal immobilization procedure (See Page 113)
C-Spine immobilization is not indicated for penetrating trauma unless a neurological deficit is noted on assessment
Assess for hemodynamic instability and follow shock protocol if indicated
Head and neck injuries:
Determine the need for C-Spine immobilization
Chest injuries:
Control bleeding
Stabilize impaled objects without removing them
Cover open chest wounds with occlusive dressing
Evaluate the back for wounds (potential for entrance/exit of GSW)
Abdominal injuries:
Control bleeding
Stabilize impaled objects
Cover eviscerations with moist, sterile gauze
Extremity injuries:
Splint according to injury type and location
Apply sterile dressings to open fractures.  Do not replace exposed bone.
Control bleeding with direct pressure and/ or tourniquet
Do not attempt to reduce dislocations in the field
Pregnant patients:
If major trauma to the abdomen, suspect life-threatening injuries
In general, the fluid filled uterus protects the fetus from blunt trauma, but these patients should be transported for evaluation.
Direct trauma may result in premature separation of the placenta from the uterine wall, premature labor, uterine rupture, abortion, or fetal death.
Place patient in left lateral recumbent position
When determining receiving facility, trauma takes precedent over the patient’s OB hospital of choice.
Advanced Care:
Establish IV/IO access with isotonic crystalloid solution to keep vein open
Consider a 2nd IV site for fluid resuscitation if signs of decompensation or hypotension
Paramedic:
Begin advanced airway management if indicated (Page 39)
Initiate continuous cardiac monitoring
Consider pain management protocol as appropriate with Fentanyl or Ketamine (Page 51)
Consider needle thoracostomy for suspected pneumothorax (Page 109)
Significant bleeding:
Administer TXA 2g IV/IO slow push
Significant crush injury, suspected rhabdomyolysis
Administer Sodium Bicarbonate 1mEq/Kg (Max 50 mEq) slow IV push
Monitor ECG before and after freeing patient from crushing injury
If hyperkalemia develops
Administer Calcium Chloride 1Gm IV/IO slow IV push
Indications:
Inadequate tissue perfusion manifesting as signs of hypoperfusion, including hypotension.
Basic Care:
- Manage airway, breathing, and oxygenation as indicated.
- For suspected trauma, fully expose patient and control external bleeding.
- Place patient in supine position or recovery position as indicated and tolerated by patient.
- Titrate oxygen to a SpO2 of >94%; for COPD patients, consider titrating to SpO2 of 88-92%.
- Obtain complete set of vital signs; including SpO2 and blood glucose.  Consider additional testing (e.g., 12-lead ECG) and monitoring (e.g., capnography) as indicated.
- Consider causes of shock that have specific treatment protocols, including:
Poisoning/Overdose
Anaphylaxis
Symptomatic bradycardia
Adrenal crisis (acute adrenal insufficiency)
Tension pneumothorax
Advanced Care:
- Initiate advanced airway management as indicated and be prepared for post-intubation hypotension.
- Fluid Resuscitation:
When indicated, administer 10-20 mL/kg isotonic crystalloid solution IV/IO.  Repeat x1 as needed.  Contact medical control for additional fluid bolus orders.
Frequently reassess and titrate to resolved hypotension and improved perfusion (e.g., more alert, decreased capillary refill).
Discontinue fluids if patient develops sign/symptoms of volume overload (e.g., new/worsening tachypnea, SOA, decreasing SpO2, new/worsening rales/crackles).
Paramedic:
- Norepinephrine Infusion:
Consider norepinephrine infusion, when distributive shock (e.g., sepsis) is suspected, other causes with specific treatment protocols have been considered/utilized, if there’s no improvement of hypotension/hypoperfusion with fluid resuscitation or the patient continues to deteriorate.
Frequently reassess and titrate to resolved hypotension.
See infusion chart Page
-TXA:
If catastrophic hemorrhage of medical origin is present, such as active GI or vaginal bleeding
Administer TXA 2g IV/IO slow push
Special Considerations:
- Patients in 2nd/3rd trimester of pregnancy are at risk of developing supine hypotensive syndrome.  Consider placing in recovery position or manually displacing uterus to patient’s left.
- For shock resulting from trauma below the neck, especially penetrating trauma, consider titrating fluid resuscitation to the lower normal limit of the blood pressure range (e.g., 90 mmHg for 11-17 yo and adults).
- The elderly and patients taking cardiovascular medications (e.g., beta blockers, calcium channel blockers) have less compensatory tachycardia in response to shock and can deteriorate quickly.
- Adult patients with poorly controlled chronic HTN can have relative hypotension, which is a state of hypoperfusion at SBPs >90 mmHg.  Consider incrementally titrating to SBPs greater than 90 mmHg.
Indications:
Patient is in cardiac arrest that is believed to be traumatic in nature
Basic Care:
If patient presentation meets requirements outlined in Withholding Resuscitative Measures protocol (Page 9), do NOT attempt resuscitation
Pregnant female at / more than 24 weeks estimated gestation or uterine fundus palpable above the umbilicus:
Initiate IMMEDIATE TRANSPORT to nearest hospital with OBGYN services (Preferably level 1 trauma center if other trauma is present)
Follow additional protocol for resuscitation en route to facility
In all other cases: Begin CPR immediately
Apply AED and perform a rhythm analysis as soon as possible while limiting interruptions in CPR for analysis / shock period only
Insert blind supraglottic airway device (I-gel) and provide ventilations with continuous EtCO2 monitoring
Control external hemorrhage
Use tourniquets if needed
Apply pelvic binder for blunt trauma, if indicated
Apply Lucas device after 2nd rhythm analysis/ shock period and set to deliver continuous compressions
Advanced Care:
Place patient on 3-lead ECG for continuous monitoring
Analyze patient at 2-minute intervals and follow AED prompts for defibrillation
Establish IV/IO access with isotonic crystalloid solution to keep vein open
Provide Epinephrine 1mg (1:10000) IV/ IO every 3-5 minutes for duration of arrest period
Initiate fluid bolus 500 mL
Consider non-traumatic causes / treatments as warranted
Paramedic:
Treat severe hemorrhagic shock as indicated above
Severe bleeding:
Administer TXA 2g IV/IO slow push
Treat obstructive shock
Perform needle thoracostomy as indicated for tension pneumothorax
Perform rhythm analysis after every 2 minutes of continuous CPR
For ventricular fibrillation/ ventricular tachycardia
Defibrillate as soon as rhythm identified
Consider Amiodarone for recurrent v-tach, Calcium for Hyperkalemia, Lidocaine if V-tach persists after Amiodarone, or Magnesium for Torsades.  See Pharmacopeia for more.
Initiate transport to Level 1 trauma center
For Asystole or pulseless electrical activity with rate <40 BPM
Continue CPR without defibrillation
If no change / improvement following 20 minutes of continuous care:
Contact medical control per Termination of Efforts protocol (See page 10)
If ROSC achieved:
Follow ROSC protocol (See Page 38)
Initiate transport to Level 1 trauma center
Perform endotracheal intubation and utilize ventilator
Ensure hemorrhage control
Ensure bilateral chest rise and fall
Consider repeat chest decompression
Consider repeat fluid bolus

Indications:
Non-traumatic abdominal pain including:
Appendicitis
Severe constipation
Abdominal Aortic Aneurysm
Gastroenteritis
Bowel Obstruction
Pancreatitis
Abdominal pain may be the first warning sign of catastrophic internal bleeding (ruptured aneurysm, liver, spleen, ectopic pregnancy, perforated abdominal viscus, etc.) Since the bleeding is not apparent, you must think of volume depletion and monitor the patient closely to recognize shock.
Basic Care:
Consult age based guide, such as Handtevy app, for appropriate medication doses/interventions/equipment sizes and reference to normal vital sign ranges for pediatric patients
Administer oxygen if indicated - Titrate to >95% and improved work of breathing
Consider possible causes and follow other protocols as appropriate
Assess for hemodynamic instability, follow shock protocols if appropriate
Advanced Care:
Establish IV/IO access with isotonic crystalloid solution to keep vein open
For mild to moderate nausea/ vomiting:
Administer Ondanestron 0.1mg/kg OR 4mg SL (if >4 years of age)
May repeat x 1 after 10 minutes not to exceed 4mg total
Paramedic:
Moderate to severe acute pain >6 on pain scale
Consider pain management protocol
Administer Fentanyl 1mcg/kg IV OR 1.5mcg/kg IN (max single dose 50mcg) (May repeat x 1 after 10 minutes)
OR Ketamine 0.3mg/kg IV/IO (May repeat x 1 after 10 minutes)
Indications:
Anaphylaxis is a life-threatening emergency that develops over minutes to several hours after allergen exposure and often involves:
Skin: hives, itching, flushing.
Airway / Respiratory: swollen lips/tongue/mucosal membranes, stridor, difficulty swallowing, SOA, wheezing.
Cardiovascular: hypotension with known allergen exposure.
Basic Care:
Consult age-based guide, such as Handtevy app, for appropriate medication doses/interventions/equipment sizes and reference to normal vital sign ranges for pediatric patients
Manage airway, breathing, and oxygenation as indicated.
Epinephrine is the most effective treatment for anaphylaxis. Aside from oxygen, epinephrine administration should not be delayed for delivery of other medications in this protocol.
Obtain complete set of vital signs, including SpO2.  Consider additional testing (e.g., 12-lead ECG) and monitoring (e.g., capnography) as indicated.
Remove inciting agent (e.g., bee stinger), if possible.
For anaphylaxis with airway/respiratory involvement or hypotension with exposure to known allergen:
Administer Epinephrine (1:1000)
<30 kg: 0.15 mg of 1:1000 concentration IM.  Repeat x2 every 5-10 minutes, as needed.
≥30 kg: 0.30 mg of 1:1000 concentration IM.  Repeat x2 every 5-10 minutes, as needed.
Contact medical control for additional doses.
For Wheezing/ Bronchospasm:
Administer 2.5 mg albuterol (0.5% concentration) nebulized.  Repeat x1 after 5 minutes, as needed.
Advanced Care:
Establish IV/IO access with isotonic crystalloid solution to keep vein open
Paramedic:
Initiate advanced airway management as indicated and anticipate airway will be difficult to manage.

protocols.title: Epinephrine
protocols.content:
Indicated for anaphylaxis with airway/respiratory involvement or hypotension with exposure to known allergen or recent (minutes) exposure to know allergen with high-risk features (e.g., history of near fatal or biphasic anaphylaxis, asthma/COPD, cardiovascular disease).
Patient weight <30 kg: 0.15 mg of 1:1,000 concentration IM.  Repeat x2 every 5-10 minutes, as needed.
Patient weight ≥30 kg: 0.30 mg of 1:1,000 concentration IM.  Repeat x2 every 5-10 minutes, as needed.
Contact medical control for additional doses.
- Epinephrine Infusion:
Anaphylaxis with impending airway/respiratory compromise or cardiovascular collapse or profound shock/hypotension that’s refractory to ≥2 IM epinephrine doses and fluid bolus.
Patient weight <30 kg: infuse at 0.1-1.0 mcg/min. (see Epinephrine Infusion protocol Page 133).
Patient weight ≥30 kg: infuse at 1.0-10.0 mcg/min (see Epinephrine Infusion protocol Page 133).
- Nebulized albuterol / ipratropium:
Indicated for wheezing /bronchospasm.
2.5 mg albuterol (0.5% concentration) and 0.5 mg ipratropium (0.02% concentration) nebulized.
Repeat albuterol treatments x3 every 5-10 minutes, as needed.
- Fluid Resuscitation:
When indicated, administer 10-20 mL/kg isotonic crystalloid solution IV/IO (repeat x1 as needed).
Contact medical control for additional fluid bolus orders.
Frequently reassess and titrate to resolved hypotension and improved perfusion (e.g., more alert, decreased capillary refill).
Discontinue fluids if patient develops sign/symptoms of volume overload (e.g., new/worsening tachypnea, SOA, decreasing SpO2, new/worsening rales/crackles).

protocols.title: Diphenhydramine
protocols.content:
Indicated for skin signs/symptoms.  Should never delay administration of epinephrine.
1 mg/kg IV/IO/IM.  Max dose 50 mg.
- Methylprednisolone:
Relatively slow-acting medication that can be considered for in addition to other therapies.  Should never delay administration of epinephrine.
2 mg/kg IV/IO.
Patient weight <30 kg: max dose 60 mg.
Patient weight ≥30 kg: max dose 125 mg.
Indications:
Exposure to toxic substances from:
○ Ingestion
○ Inhalation
○ Injection
○ Skin absorption
○ Intentional/accidental exposure to pharmacological substances
Other medical conditions (see below) causing altered mental status
Basic Care:
Remove patient from toxic environment as quickly as possible, remove clothing, and decontaminate if applicable
○ This should be performed by trained personnel with appropriate PPE
Administer oxygen
○ Titrate to ≥95% and work of breathing
○ Assist ventilations as appropriate
Initiate continuous EtCO2 monitoring
Follow other protocols as appropriate
○ Diabetic Emergencies
○ Hypothermia/Hyperthermia
○ Seizures/Status Epilepticus
○ Stroke/CVA/TIA
○ Trauma
○ Agitated/Aggressive Patient
Use patient and/or bystander statements and answers to determine if/what substances are involved
Determine blood glucose concentration and if <60mg/dL
○ Administer oral glucose 15g buccal, if conscious and able to tolerate
If unable to tolerate oral glucose AND PATIENT HAS A PRESCRIPTION
▪ Administer Glucagon 0.1mg/kg IM (Max 1mg)
Suspected opiate/opioid overdose
○ Administer naloxone 0.1mg/kg IN
May administer additional Naloxone 0.1mg/kg IN every 5 minutes to restore respiratory drive to max total 2mg
Suspected carbon monoxide exposure
○ Monitor CO level if possible
○ Administer high-flow oxygen at 15LPM
Advanced Care:
Establish IV/IO access with isotonic crystalloid solution to keep vein open
Blood glucose concentration is <60mg/dL
○ Administer dextrose 10% 4ml/kg  IV/IO
May repeat x1 if no response
IV access cannot be obtained
○ Administer Glucagon 0.1mg/kg IM (Max 1mg)
Suspected opiate/opioid overdose
○ Administer Naloxone 0.1mg/kg IV every 5 minutes to restore respiratory drive to Max total 2mg
Paramedic:
Begin advanced airway management as appropriate
Initiate cardiac monitoring
If signs of shock refer to Shock protocols
Patient exhibits signs of organophosphate poisoning
○ Administer Atropine 0.02mg/kg  IV/IO
▪ Repeat at 0.02mg/kg every 3 minutes fully atropinized (secretions dried)
Suspected TCA overdose
○ Administer Sodium Bicarbonate 1mEq/kg  IV/IO
Suspected beta-blocker overdose
○ Administer Glucagon 0.7mg/kg  IV/IO
▪ May repeat x1 to max of 5mg
Suspected calcium channel-blocker overdose
○ Administer Calcium chloride 20mg/kg  IV/IO (Max 1g)
May repeat x 1 after 10 minutes
Suspected dystonic reaction
○ Administer Diphenhydramine 1mg/kg (Max 50mg) IV/IO/IM
Suspected adrenal crisis
AMS, hypoglycemia, hypotension, seizures, arrhythmias
Administer Solu-Medrol 2mg/kg IV/IO/IM
Indications:
An apparent life-threatening event (ALTE) is defined as an episode that is frightening to the observer and is characterized by some combination of:
Apnea
Color change
Marked change in muscle tone
Unexplained choking or gagging
A brief resolved unexplained event (BRUE) is similar to ALTE but symptoms resolve without intervention
Basic Care:
Consult age based guide, such as Handtevy app, for appropriate medication doses/interventions/equipment sizes and reference to normal vital sign ranges for pediatric patients
Provide emotional support to parents
Document all aspects of scene and environmental conditions
If Sudden Infant Death Syndrome (SIDS) is suspected, consult cardiac arrest protocols (See Page 79)
Monitor ABC’s and assessment using the Pediatric Assessment Triangle
Measure and record temperature
Blow-by oxygen as tolerated
Pulse oximetry for reported apneic events
Determine blood glucose concentration
ALL infants who have experienced an ALTE or BRUE must be transported to the appropriate children’s hospital
(Ped. Assessment Triangle)
Indications:
Exacerbation of previously diagnosed asthma
Characterized by some combination of:
Wheezing
Tachypnea
Accessory muscle use / retraction
Inability to speak in full sentences
Wheezing due to suspected asthma (>1 year of age)
Basic Care:
Consult age based guide, such as Handtevy app, for appropriate medication doses/interventions/equipment sizes and reference to normal vital sign ranges for pediatric patients
Administer oxygen
Titrate to >95% and improved work of breathing
Initiate continuous EtCO2 monitoring
Wheezing/ bronchospasm:
Administer 0.5% Albuterol 2.5mg
May repeat x
May co-administer with 0.02% Ipratropium Bromide 0.5mg
Moderate to severe respiratory distress
Assist ventilations as necessary
Advanced Care:
Moderate to severe respiratory distress:
Initiate CPAP per CPAP procedure
If signs of impending respiratory failure prior to or following administration of CPAP, proceed to assisted ventilations with BVM
Discontinue CPAP if patient becomes hypotensive
Establish IV/IO access with isotonic crystalloid solution to keep vein open
Additional DuoNeb doses may be given by the A-EMT as long as wheezing is present every 5 minutes to max of 3 additional doses
Paramedic:
Initiate cardiac monitoring
Subacute presentation
Administer methylprednisolone 2mg/kg  IV/IO  - Max 125mg
Administer magnesium sulfate 50mg/kg (max 2g) infused over 10 minutes
Unable to cooperate/ tolerate nebulizer therapy or impending respiratory failure:
Administer Epinephrine (1:1000) 0.15mg IM
May repeat x 1 after 5 minutes
Symptoms increase in severity and respiratory failure suspected:
Initiate Pediatric Respiratory Distress or Failure protocol (See p.83)
Indications:
Heart rate is less than age-appropriate rate with a pulse and signs of hypoperfusion, including hypotension
Pediatric symptomatic bradycardia most commonly results from inadequate oxygenation/ ventilation
Basic Care:
Manage airway, breathing, and oxygenation as indicated
Titrate oxygen to a SpO2 > 95%
Begin / continue CPR for pediatric patients with a heart rate < 60 bpm and signs of hypoperfusion despite adequate oxygenation / ventilation
Place patient in supine or recovery position as indicated and tolerated by patient
Obtain a complete set of vital signs, including: SpO2 and blood glucose concentration.
Advanced Care:
Initiate cardiac monitoring and obtain a 12-lead ECG if possible
Establish IV / IO access with isotonic crystalloid solution to keep vein open
Paramedic:
Initiate advanced airway management as indicated and be prepared for post-intubation hypotension and/or worsening bradycardia.
Transcutaneous pacing:
Contact medical control for pediatric transcutaneous pacing order.
TCP in pediatric patients should be considered if:
Reversible causes (e.g., hypoxia, hypoglycemia, opioid overdose) and medications (e.g., atropine, epinephrine) have been considered/delivered without desired effect.
Presence of 2nd degree Mobitz type II or 3rd degree heart block or patient has had a heart transplant.
Consider sedation prior to TCP, if the patient isn’t at risk of impending cardiovascular collapse, or if purposeful movement affects TCP
Recommended initial settings to request orders for:
Mode: syn/demand
Rate:
<1 yo: 120 bpm
1-10 yo: 100 bpm
≥11 yo: 80 bpm
Current: start low and increase by 5-10 mA until mechanical capture is achieved (usually 40-80 mA).
Generally, the above listed heart rates are enough to produce adequate perfusion.
If capture not achieved at current of 110 mA, consider repositioning pads and additional/alternative treatments.
Special Considerations:

protocols.title: Epinephrine
protocols.content:
First-line medication for pediatric symptomatic bradycardia.
0.01 mg/kg IV/IO slow IVP.  Repeat every 3-5 minutes as needed.

protocols.title: Atropine
protocols.content:
Indicated for symptomatic bradycardia due to increased vagal tone +/- 1st degree heart block.
Ineffective for heart transplant patients, bradycardia due to hypoxia, 3rd degree heart block, and usually 2nd degree heart block.
0.02 mg/kg IV/IO (min single dose 0.1 mg, total max dose 1 mg).  Repeat every 3-5 minutes, as needed.
- Fluid Resuscitation:
IV fluids can be used to treat hypotension (see Hypoperfusion page 80), but should not delay or replace epinephrine or treatments that directly target suspected causes of bradycardia (e.g., atropine for increased vagal tone).
When indicated, administer 10-20 mL/kg Isotonic crystalloid IV/IO (repeat x1 as needed). Contact medical control for additional fluid bolus orders.
- Situations where additional/alternative treatments are often needed, include:
Beta blocker overdose:
Glucagon 0.05 mg/kg IV/IO (max single 5 mg) given over 1 minute.  Contact medical control for additional doses.
Calcium channel blocker overdose:
Calcium chloride 20 mg/kg IV/IO slow IVP.  Contact medical control for additional doses.
Hyperkalemia:
Calcium chloride 20 mg/kg IV/IO slow IVP.  Contact medical control for additional doses.
Sodium bicarbonate (8.4% solution) 1 mEq/kg IV/IO (4.2% solution recommended for <1 month old).  Repeat x1 in 5-10 minutes, as needed.
Severe / prolonged acidosis or sodium channel blocker overdose:
Sodium bicarbonate (8.4% solution) 1 mEq/kg IV/IO (4.2% solution recommended for <1 month old).  Repeat x1 in 5-10 minutes, as needed.
Symptomatic bradycardia refractory to TCP and/or other treatments:
Consider epinephrine infusion 0.1-1.0 mcg/min (see Epinephrine Infusion protocol page 132).
or
Consider push-dose Epinephrine 1 mcg/kg slow IVP over 2 minutes.  Repeat every 3-5 minutes, as needed
Indications:
When the upper airway is infected with the virus that causes croup, tissues around the voice box (larynx) and the windpipe (trachea) will swell.
When a cough forces air through this narrowed passageway, it may sound like a seal barking.
Fever
Hoarse voice
Noisy or labored breathing
Often worse at night
Basic Care:
Consult age-based guide, such as Handtevy app, for appropriate medication doses/interventions/equipment sizes and reference to normal vital sign ranges for pediatric patients
Administer oxygen
Titrate to >95% and improved work of breathing
Consider humidified oxygen for mild symptoms
Initiate EtCO2 monitoring
Remove any tight clothing
Allow patient to remain in a position of comfort with someone familiar
The condition of an upset patient can deteriorate quicker than that of a calm patient
Family should be used to soothe the patient and keep them calm if possible
Do not force the patient into a position, they will protect their airway by their positioning
Evaluation should include temperature
Passive cooling if patient found to be febrile
Advanced Care:
Establish IV/IO access with isotonic crystalloid solution to keep vein open
Initiate cardiac monitoring if possible
Paramedic:
For severe respiratory distress:
Administer nebulized epinephrine (1:1000) 3mg mixed with 3ml isotonic crystalloid solution
Basic Care:
Consult age-based guide, such as Handtevy app, for appropriate medication doses/interventions/equipment sizes and reference to normal vital sign ranges for pediatric patients
Administer oxygen
Titrate to >95% and improved work of breathing
Initiate continuous EtCO2 monitoring
Determine blood glucose concentration
Relatively or clinically hypoglycemic without concern for aspiration
Administer oral glucose 15g buccal
May repeat every 5 minutes as needed
Advanced Care & Paramedic:
Establish IV/IO access with isotonic crystalloid solution to keep vein open
Hyperglycemia:
Consider 250-500 ml fluid bolus as appropriate if no concern for respiratory status or pulmonary edema
Hypoglycemia:
Use D5W if available for IV/IO access
Administer Dextrose 10% 4ml/kg  IV/IO
OR if IV/IO access cannot be obtained, administer Glucagon
0.1 mg/kg (max 1mg) IM
Basic Care:
Consult age-based guide, such as Handtevy app, for appropriate medication doses/interventions/equipment sizes and reference to normal vital sign ranges for pediatric patients
Rectal temperature is the preferred method of obtaining core temperature in children
Begin passive cooling, remove excessive clothing/ blankets
Do not cool to induce shivering
Follow Pediatric Seizure protocol if febrile seizure is suspected
For temperatures > 100.5⁰ F
If a child has had Acetaminophen more than 4 hours prior
Administer Acetaminophen 15mg/kg PO (Max single dose 500mg)
If the last dose of Acetaminophen was less than 4 hours prior and the child has not had Ibuprofen in the previous 6 hours
Administer Ibuprofen 10mg/kg PO (Max single dose 300mg)
Contraindicated in children under 6 months of age
Indications:
Elevated body temperature related to heat exposure
Altered mental status related to heat exposure
Basic Care:
Consult age-based guide, such as Handtevy app, for appropriate medication doses/interventions/equipment sizes and reference to normal vital sign ranges for pediatric patients
Administer oxygen
Titrate to >95% and improved work of breathing
Initiate continuous EtCO2 monitoring
Move patient to a cool place away from any external heat sources if possible
Obtain patient temperature (rectal temperature is preferred in pediatrics if available)
Mild symptoms: (heat cramps, heat exhaustion, no signs of AMS, body temperature is <104 ⁰F
Help facilitate passive cooling
Loosen clothing, remove excessive clothing/ blankets
Administer PO fluids (if available and patient tolerates)
Discontinue if report of nausea/ vomiting
Determine blood glucose concentration
Severe symptoms: (signs of AMS, body temperature >104⁰ F, patient may or may not be sweating)
Begin active cooling
Transport may be delayed for on-scene cold water immersion if possible
Use sheets or towels dipped in ice water on exposed skin
Place ice packs behind neck, in axillae, and in groin areas
Advanced Care:
Establish IV/IO access with isotonic crystalloid solution to keep vein open
Initiate IV/IO fluid bolus 20ml/kg for hypotension
Paramedic:
Uncontrolled shivering during cooling
Administer Midazolam 0.1mg/kg (Max 1mg) IV/IO/IM/IN
Indications:
Decreased body temperature related to cold exposure
Altered mental status related to cold exposure
Repeated ACLS medications and repeated defibrillations are ineffective below 86 degrees Fahrenheit (Core temperature)
Basic Care:
Consult age-based guide, such as Handtevy app, for appropriate medication doses/interventions/equipment sizes and reference to normal vital sign ranges for pediatric patients
Administer oxygen
Titrate to >95% and improved work of breathing
Initiate continuous EtCO2 monitoring
Decrease on-going heat loss ASAP
Move the patient to a warm area
Dry and insulate the patient
Handle the patient gently, allowing the patient no exertion
Rough handling of a severely hypothermic patient may induce ventricular fibrillation
Remove all wet clothing (cut off to decrease patient movement)
Initiate passive external warming with blankets in a warm ambulance
Utilize heat blankets from blanket warmer device if available
Obtain patient temperature (core temperature preferred if obtainable)
Suspected hypothermia:
Assess respirations and pulse carefully as both may be very slow but still adequate for patient’s slowed metabolism
Provide expeditious, non-emergency transport
Call for ALS assistance, but DO NOT DELAY TRANSPORT
Begin airway management as appropriate
Follow other protocols as appropriate
